title: Tai chi
hook: in a trial, tai chi improved balance and reduced falls more than stretching (Li et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday: yoga and back pain, and your line was stretch. Did you find ten minutes to move, any way at all? Day one thousand three hundred forty.

Early morning in a city park, a group of people move together as if they were underwater. Arms float up. Weight shifts from one foot to the other, so slowly it's hard to see where one movement ends and the next begins. Nobody is sweating. Nobody is hurrying. A jogger goes past them twice. It looks almost too gentle to do anything at all. A research team decided to put that gentleness to a test, against two other kinds of exercise, with people whose balance was at real risk.
screen: `MOVING AS IF UNDERWATER.` → `NOBODY HURRYING.` → `TOO GENTLE TO DO ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: First, what tai chi is. It's a Chinese practice of slow, flowing movement. Tradition links it to the martial arts and to Taoist ideas about softness and balance. The name, taiji in Chinese, is usually translated the supreme ultimate. Second, the trial. A team led by Fuzhong Li worked with people living with Parkinson's disease, whose steadiness on their feet was a daily worry. They compared tai chi with strength training and with stretching, over several months. Third, the result. The tai chi group improved more in balance than the other groups, and had fewer falls than the stretching group. Gentle turned out to be strong. Fourth, why slow might work, and an old echo. Tai chi keeps shifting the weight from one leg to the other under control, so it's balance practice in disguise. Going slowly makes a person pay attention to the feet, the knees, the ground. And earlier this year, reading the Tao Te Ching chapter by chapter, we met its love of the soft: water that wears down what is hard, the young plant that is supple while it lives. Tai chi takes that old idea and puts it into the hips and ankles. The lab didn't test the Tao Te Ching. It tested slow movement, and slow movement held up. Slow and steady.
screen: `SLOW, FLOWING MOVEMENT.` · `TAI CHI, STRENGTH, OR STRETCHING.` · `BETTER BALANCE, FEWER FALLS.` · `THE SOFT, IN THE HIPS AND ANKLES.` · then, large: `GENTLE TURNED OUT TO BE STRONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try slow movement. If you can stand safely, stand with your feet about hip-width apart, near something to hold. If not, stay seated. Let your knees soften. Now shift your weight slowly toward the right foot, as slowly as you can. Then slowly back to the center, and on to the left. Let your arms float a little if they want to. Feel the soles of your feet doing the work. After a few shifts, sit, and let the body be still. The bell holds the time.
Tai chi. A Chinese practice of slow movement that, in a trial, improved balance and reduced falls more than stretching. Today's word.
Your line: slow and steady. Today, do one ordinary movement at half speed, like climbing the stairs or carrying a cup, and feel your feet the whole way. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

howItsDone: People practice tai chi alone or in groups, often outdoors in parks, moving slowly through a set sequence of forms; some community and hospital programs teach it for balance.
